# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

This dissertation set out to answer if Deep Gaussian Processes improve on single-layer GPs for real-world machine learning tasks, and if so, when and at what cost? The theoretical development, from weight-space Bayesian linear regression through the kernel trick, GP inference, and doubly stochastic variational inference, established the machinery required to make this question tractable at scale. Two experiments then tested the practical implications.

## Key Findings

**DGPs outperform single-layer GPs only on non-stationary, compositional targets.** On the Kin8nm robot kinematics benchmark, DSVGP-2L reduced RMSE by 10.7% over SVGP (0.0699 vs 0.0783) and improved NLPD from $-1.116$ to $-1.241$. The improvement is theoretically coherent: Kin8nm's target is a composition of trigonometric functions of joint angles, precisely the hierarchical non-linearity where learned intermediate representations add value. On the UCI credit card default benchmark, where the target surface is smoother and more monotonic, DGPs matched but did not exceed single-layer GP performance. This contrast directly supports the theoretical prediction by @damianou_deep_2013 that DGP depth is only beneficial when the underlying function is non-stationary and compositional.

**The GP family delivers substantially better native probability calibration than classical models.** On the credit card classification task, GP models achieved ECE of 0.010–0.021, compared to 0.087–0.225 for random forest, XGBoost, and logistic regression — a 4–22$\times$ improvement requiring no post-hoc calibration. This calibration advantage held across all training set sizes from 425 observations onward. For regulatory applications under Basel IRB, where PD estimates must track observed default frequencies across rating grades, this property is practically significant: XGBoost's miscalibration would likely require post-hoc recalibration while GP models' native calibration is consistent with these standards.

**DSVGP-3L consistently fails to justify its cost.** Across both datasets and all training scales, three-layer DGPs never outperformed two-layer variants on any metric. At small training set sizes ($N \leq 500$), DSVGP-3L degraded catastrophically — R² = 0.002 on Kin8nm small scale and ROC-AUC = 0.523 on UCI small scale — before recovering at medium scale. At full scale, the extra layer adds approximately $3.6\times$ training time with no measurable gain. DSVGP-2L is consequently the more defensible deep configuration: it achieves the benefits of depth when they exist, without the instability and cost of deeper architectures.

## Limitations

These findings are subject to several limitations. First, all experiments were conducted on CPU (Apple M2) without GPU acceleration; absolute training times would be considerably shorter on modern hardware, though relative ratios between models would remain approximately the same. Second, only two datasets were evaluated — a broader benchmark study across more domains would be needed to establish stronger generalisability claims. Third, the DGP architectures tested use fixed-width hidden layers with a single hidden dimension; variable-width or residual DGP architectures [@salimbeni_doubly_2017] were not explored. Finally, the regulatory compliance claims are illustrative rather than definitive: real-world PD model validation involves back-testing, portfolio-level stability testing, and model documentation requirements that go beyond the metrics evaluated here.

## Future Directions

Several directions extend naturally from this work. Stochastic-depth DGPs [@duvenaud_avoiding_2014], which skip layers stochastically during training, may address the small-data collapse of deep architectures while retaining flexibility at larger scales. Amortised variational inference could reduce the per-model training cost and enable DGPs to scale to dataset sizes where the GP training premium currently becomes prohibitive. On the application side, regulatory back-testing of GP-based PD models — evaluating stability of calibration across economic cycles and portfolio segments — would provide stronger evidence for or against adoption in practice. More broadly, combining the uncertainty quantification properties of GP classifiers with the scalability of neural-network feature extractors (deep kernel learning) represents a promising middle ground between the two model families compared in this work.

The central lesson is that the right level of model complexity is determined by the structure of the target function, not by theoretical expressiveness alone. DGPs add genuine value when the problem demands it; when it does not, the simpler GP is preferable.
